promptText: What is the purpose of a validation set, as distinct from a training set and a test set?
options: It is used repeatedly during development to tune hyperparameters and other engineering choices, while the test set is touched only once at the very end
It is identical in purpose to the test set and the two terms are interchangeable
It is used to compute the loss function's mathematical formula
It is discarded entirely before training begins and never used again
explanation: The training set is what the model learns from, the validation set is iterated on freely to tune choices like hyperparameters, and the test set is checked only once to produce an honest, unbiased estimate of real-world performance.

options: A model that is too simple to capture the real underlying pattern in the data
A model that learns the training data too specifically, including its noise, so it performs well on training data but poorly on new, unseen data
A model that trains slower than expected on the available hardware
A model with too few parameters to represent the task
explanation: Overfitting is the opposite of the actual goal, generalization — the model has memorized quirks specific to its training sample rather than learning patterns that transfer to new data.

promptText: Why is accuracy a misleading default metric on a highly imbalanced dataset, such as one where fraud is 0.1% of all cases?
options: Accuracy cannot be mathematically computed on imbalanced data at all
A model that always predicts the majority class ('not fraud') achieves very high accuracy while being completely useless at catching the minority class that actually matters
Imbalanced datasets always produce exactly 0% accuracy regardless of the model
Accuracy is a valid metric only for regression problems, never for classification
explanation: A classifier that always says 'not fraud' scores 99.9% accuracy while catching zero real fraud cases — precision, recall, and F1 exist specifically to expose this failure mode that accuracy hides.

promptText: What does cross-entropy loss specifically penalize more heavily than an uncertain, wrong prediction?
options: Any prediction that is ultimately correct
A confident prediction that turns out to be wrong
A prediction that takes longer to compute
A prediction made using fewer input features
explanation: Cross-entropy operates on a logarithmic scale, so a confident-and-wrong prediction (e.g., 99% probability for the wrong class) is punished far more heavily than an uncertain-and-wrong one (e.g., 51% probability).

promptText: What is self-supervised learning, and why is it central to how large language models are pre-trained?
options: It requires a human to manually label every single training example before training starts
It generates 'labels' automatically from the structure of unlabeled data itself (e.g., the next word in a sentence), removing the need for expensive human annotation at massive scale
It only works on image data and cannot be applied to text
It replaces labels entirely with rewards from a reinforcement learning signal
explanation: For LLMs, the label is simply the next word and the input is everything before it — a label that already exists for free in any text corpus, which is why pretraining scales to trillions of tokens without human labeling.

promptText: According to the bias-variance decomposition, total expected error is approximately composed of which three terms?
options: Bias squared, plus variance, plus irreducible noise
Only bias, with variance and noise being negligible in practice
Only variance, since bias can always be reduced to zero with enough data
The learning rate squared, plus the batch size
explanation: Bias is systematic error from a model too simple to capture the pattern, variance is error from sensitivity to the specific training sample, and irreducible noise is randomness inherent to the problem that no model can predict away.

promptText: Why must feature scaling/normalization statistics (mean, standard deviation) be computed only on the training set, not the full dataset, before splitting?
options: It is purely a compute-time optimization with no effect on correctness
Computing them on the full dataset lets validation/test data subtly influence training-time statistics, a form of leakage that makes reported performance optimistically biased
Scaling has no measurable effect on model performance in any circumstance
It is required only as a legal compliance step in regulated industries
explanation: If scaling statistics are derived from the full dataset, the training process indirectly 'knows' something about the validation/test distribution, inflating measured performance in a way that won't hold in production.

promptText: Why is a random train/test split inappropriate for time-series data, and what should be used instead?
options: Random splits are always perfectly fine for time-series data
A random split can put future data in the training set and past data in the test set, letting the model implicitly 'see the future' — a time-based or walk-forward split should be used instead
Time-series data cannot be split into training and test sets under any methodology
Random splits only fail for classification problems, never for regression
explanation: This produces unrealistically good offline performance that can't survive contact with production, where the future genuinely isn't available yet — walk-forward validation keeps training data chronologically prior to validation data.

promptText: Comparing random forests and gradient boosting: what is fundamentally different about how each combines its trees?
options: They are functionally identical and differ only in their implementation library

Random forests build many trees independently in parallel and average them, primarily reducing variance; gradient boosting builds trees sequentially, each one correcting the errors of the ensemble built so far, primarily reducing bias
Gradient boosting cannot use decision trees as its base learner
Random forests train exactly one tree total, unlike gradient boosting
explanation: Random forests reduce variance through averaging over independent, decorrelated trees, while boosting reduces bias by iteratively focusing capacity on whatever the ensemble is still getting wrong.

promptText: Why does L1 regularization tend to produce sparse (exactly zero) coefficients, while L2 regularization does not?
options: L1 is simply computed faster on modern hardware than L2
Geometrically, the L1 penalty's constraint region has sharp corners located on the coordinate axes, where the optimal solution tends to land; L2's smooth circular region rarely produces an exact zero
L2 regularization always removes more features from the model than L1 does
L1 regularization is mathematically incompatible with linear models
explanation: This is a geometric consequence of the shape of each penalty, not an arbitrary design choice — L1's corners on the axes are where coefficients land exactly at zero, effectively performing feature selection.

promptText: What two mechanisms does the Adam optimizer combine, and why does this make it robust with relatively little manual tuning?
options: A fixed learning rate schedule combined with no gradient information at all
Momentum (a running average of past gradients, smoothing direction) combined with a per-parameter adaptive learning rate (based on a running average of squared gradients)
Two independent copies of plain SGD trained separately and averaged together
L1 and L2 regularization applied simultaneously to every weight
explanation: This combination scales down steps for parameters receiving large or noisy gradients and scales up steps for parameters receiving small, consistent gradients, which is why Adam converges quickly and robustly across many architectures.

promptText: Why might two models with identical aggregate benchmark scores behave very differently in your specific production application?
options: Identical benchmark scores mathematically guarantee identical behavior in every downstream application

Aggregate scores average performance across many question types and can hide very different strength/weakness profiles, and benchmarks don't capture things like verbosity, tone, latency, or behavior under your specific prompt structure
Benchmark scores for language models are generated randomly and carry no real signal
This situation is a purely theoretical edge case that never actually occurs in practice
explanation: Two models can arrive at the same overall number through very different profiles — one excelling at factual recall, another at formatting compliance — which is exactly why a representative in-house evaluation set should drive the final choice.

promptText: A model shows 99% training accuracy and 65% validation accuracy. What is the correct diagnosis, and what is the right order of fixes to try?
options: This is underfitting; the correct fix is to add more model capacity immediately
This is a textbook high-variance/overfitting signature; fixes in rough cost order are: add or strengthen regularization, simplify the model, gather more/diverse data, and audit for data leakage
This indicates the loss function itself is broken and must be replaced entirely
This pattern is normal and healthy and requires no corrective action
explanation: The large gap between near-perfect training accuracy and much lower validation accuracy is the classic sign the model has memorized the training set rather than learning generalizable patterns.

promptText: Why is nested cross-validation needed specifically when a workflow requires both hyperparameter selection and an honest final performance estimate?
options: It isn't actually needed — plain k-fold cross-validation is always sufficient for both purposes

Selecting hyperparameters using the same folds you later report performance on lets those 'test' folds subtly influence the hyperparameter choice, a form of leakage that optimistically biases the final estimate; nesting keeps selection and estimation honestly separated
Nested cross-validation is a technique reserved exclusively for deep learning models
Nested cross-validation eliminates the need to hold out any validation data at all
explanation: An outer loop estimates generalization performance while an inner loop selects hyperparameters within each outer fold's training data, at the cost of significantly more compute, but keeping the final number honest.

promptText: Why might an LLM-as-judge evaluation be an unreliable substitute for ground truth, despite being far more scalable than human review?
options: LLM judges are mathematically proven to be more accurate than any human rater in every scenario

An LLM judge is itself a probabilistic system that can be swayed by response length or confident tone and shares many failure modes with the model it's grading, so it isn't an independent oracle and should be periodically validated against a human-labeled sample
LLM judges are physically incapable of processing text longer than a single sentence
LLM-as-judge evaluation is mathematically identical to exact-match unit testing
explanation: Because the judge is trained on a similar distribution of 'what sounds right' as the model it evaluates, it can be inconsistent on borderline cases and biased by surface qualities, so it should be treated as a scalable signal, not an infallible oracle.
